profile.background: An adult who shares a house with two friends and volunteers to wash the team bibs for a recreational walking group. They enjoy the weekly outing.
profile.history: They recall an earlier episode of very muddled thinking and later discussions about schizophrenia at the outpatient clinic. Lately keeping track of several small tasks has felt difficult.
profile.organization: Has a general sense of the sequence of events but related thoughts can pull attention away from the point. Concrete details are easier to recall than broad summaries.
profile.spontaneity: Likes to talk and often notices extra details while remembering an event.
profile.guardedness: Open about the walking group but dislikes the impression that they cannot manage responsibilities.
profile.expression: Good-humored about minor mistakes and disappointed when an unfinished job affects someone else.
profile.self_understanding: Notices that having several things needing attention at once makes it easier to lose track.

facts.content: Before last week's walk they put the clean team bibs by the door and got distracted looking for a bus card. A friend reminded them to take the bag.
facts.disclosure_context: A little embarrassed, particularly about other people waiting.

facts.content: It is easier to lay out things for the group in the evening, when the kitchen is quiet.
facts.disclosure_context: An observation they can discuss comfortably.

facts.content: They put their bus card in the pocket of the bib bag after the last walk.
facts.disclosure_context: Pleased to have found a practical arrangement.

facts.content: A housemate sometimes reads the day's jobs back to them while they gather things.
facts.disclosure_context: Comfortable receiving help from this person.

facts.content: They keep their medication in its labeled pack and remember the next outpatient appointment because it falls the day after the group walk.
facts.disclosure_context: These are familiar details of their week.

dialogue.question: What have you been looking forward to lately?
dialogue.answer: “The walk each week, really. I go with a group, and it’s nice to get out and have a chat—we share a house, me and two friends, but it’s different getting out together. I wash the team bibs, so that’s my little job. They’re easier to get ready in the evening when the kitchen’s quiet. But yes, the walk itself—that’s what I look forward to.”

dialogue.question: What would you like to talk over while you're here?
dialogue.answer: “Lately I keep losing track when there are a few little things to do at once. I’ll start getting something ready, then something else catches my attention, and… what was I doing? (small laugh) It’s not that I can’t do the jobs. I like having my bit to do for the walking group. I just don’t like the thought of people waiting on me because I’ve left something unfinished.”

dialogue.question: When does everything get a bit much?
dialogue.answer: “Mostly when I’m getting ready to go out and there’s more than one thing to remember. Last week I had the clean bibs by the door, all ready, then I went looking for my bus card and got caught up in that. A friend reminded me about the bag. Bit embarrassing, really—it was sitting right there. In the evening, when the kitchen’s quiet, I can get things laid out more easily. It’s when everything needs attention together that I lose my place.”

dialogue.question: I mean keeping track of several jobs. Are there particular times when that feels easier or harder?
dialogue.answer: “Evenings are easier, when the kitchen’s quiet. I can lay the bibs out and finish that before doing something else. It’s harder just before we leave, especially if I’m looking for something and someone’s talking to me—I go with that and lose where I’d got to. One of my housemates sometimes reads the jobs back to me while I gather things. That helps, actually, having a reminder rather than trying to hold the whole lot in my head.”

dialogue.question: How do you usually get things together for the walking group?
dialogue.answer: “I wash the bibs and try to get them together in the evening, when the kitchen’s quiet, then leave the bag by the door. Sometimes my housemate reads the jobs back to me while I gather things. After the last walk I put my bus card in the bag’s pocket—quite pleased with that, actually. No point having the bibs ready and then hunting everywhere for the card, is there?”

dialogue.question: Could you give me an example of something you needed to remember before a recent outing?
dialogue.answer: “The bag of clean bibs, last week. I’d put it by the door, so that part was done, but then I started looking for my bus card and nearly went without the bag. My friend said, ‘Don’t forget the bibs.’ A bit embarrassing when it’s my job to bring them—I had washed them and everything, just hadn’t picked them up.”

dialogue.question: Does the order make a difference to you?
dialogue.answer: “Yes, I think so. If I get the bibs into the bag and put it by the door before starting on something else, it’s easier. If I stop halfway to look for my bus card, then I can lose where I’d got to. The card’s in the bag pocket now, actually, so that’s one less thing to hunt for. I don’t think there’s one special order—it’s more finishing one bit before I get pulled onto the next.”

dialogue.question: I mean the order in which you do your jobs. What difference does having a usual sequence make, if any?
dialogue.answer: “Oh, yes—a usual order means I’m not stopping to work out what comes next each time. Wash the bibs, get them into the bag, put it by the door. I can follow that along. If I break off halfway, I sometimes have to look through the bag again to see what I’ve actually done. The washing’s done, but have I packed them? That sort of thing. Having the same order helps me keep my place.”

dialogue.question: Who do you feel comfortable asking for help with a practical job?
dialogue.answer: “One of my housemates—we’re friends, so I don’t feel awkward asking them. Sometimes they read the day’s jobs back to me while I gather things, which helps me keep my place. I still get the things together myself, you know. It’s just useful having someone remind me what I was doing if I get sidetracked.”

dialogue.question: What do you do when two things need your attention at the same time?
dialogue.answer: “Well, sometimes I turn to the second thing and leave the first half done—that’s where I lose my place. If my housemate’s there, I’ll ask them to remind me what’s still waiting. It helps to finish one thing first, though I don’t always notice I’ve switched until I’m looking for something else. Like the bus card—the bibs were ready, but I’d stopped thinking about picking them up.”

dialogue.question: How do you remember when it's time for a clinic appointment?
dialogue.answer: “My next one’s the day after the group walk, so that helps it stick. I’ve got the walk in mind anyway, and then it’s the clinic the following day. Easier than trying to remember a date on its own—I couldn’t tell you the number off the top of my head.”

dialogue.question: Is there anything about your day-to-day life you'd like us to talk more about?
dialogue.answer: “Yes, keeping on top of my own jobs without someone having to remind me quite so much. I don’t mind my housemate helping—they’re good about it—but I like doing my share. The walking group’s something I enjoy, and I want to keep washing the bibs. It’s just those little bits between getting them washed and actually getting out the door that seem to trip me up.”
